references.text: In his answer to the Jews, the man had already referred to the one who healed him, but without being able to identify him by name – he only said that "the one who made me well" told him to take up his bed and walk ([ref:Joh 5:11|John 5:11]).
The Jews had asked who it was that had told him to take up his bed and walk, but the man did not know at that time who Jesus was ([ref:Joh 5:12-13|John 5:12-13]).
Jesus found the man in the temple and spoke to him – this meeting made it so that the man now knew who had healed him ([ref:Joh 5:14|John 5:14]).
As a direct result of the man telling the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him, the Jews began to persecute Jesus because he did this on the Sabbath ([ref:Joh 5:16|John 5:16]).
A similar situation arises when the man born blind is brought before the Pharisees after his healing – here too, Jesus' healing act is reported to the religious leaders ([ref:Joh 9:13|John 9:13]).
Also after the raising of Lazarus, some went to the Pharisees and told what Jesus had done, which led to further hostility and plans to kill him ([ref:Joh 11:46|John 11:46]).

The expression "the Jews" (οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι) is used in the Gospel of John often for the Jewish religious leaders, as here where they act as an investigating and resistant group ([ref:Joh 1:19|John 1:19]).
